fields.title: Habakkuk
fields.subtitle: Chavaqquq, “The Book of Habakkuk”
fields.description: The eighth of the twelve Minor Prophets, and the one who argues with God. Habakkuk sees violence and twisted justice in Judah and cries, “How long, LORD, must I cry for help while you do not listen?” God’s answer, that he is raising up the Babylonians, only deepens the question. So the prophet climbs to his watchpost to wait, and is told to write down a vision that will not be late, and that “the righteous will live by their faithfulness”, the line Paul made the hinge of the gospel. The book ends with a psalm of the God who comes to save, and a song of joy when the fig tree does not flower. Set out line by line as the poetry it is, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Habakkuk about?
qa.answer: The problem of evil, brought straight to God. In chapter 1 Habakkuk complains that God tolerates violence and injustice in Judah, and when God answers that he will judge Judah by means of the Babylonians, he complains again that a holy God is using a nation even more wicked. In chapter 2 God tells him the vision will come in its time, that the righteous will live by their faithfulness, and pronounces five woes on the proud oppressor. Chapter 3 is the prophet’s prayer, a psalm that ends in trust and joy.

qa.question: Who was Habakkuk, and when did he live?
qa.answer: The book calls him only “Habakkuk the prophet” (1:1; 3:1), and nothing else is known of his life; later legends about him, such as the story in the Greek additions to Daniel, are of uncertain worth. The meaning of his name is also uncertain. Because God says he is “raising up the Chaldeans” (1:6), the book is usually dated to the late seventh century BC, when Babylon was rising to power, often to the reign of Jehoiakim (609–598 BC), shortly before Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC.

qa.question: What does Habakkuk 2:4, “the righteous will live by their faithfulness”, mean?
qa.answer: In Hebrew the line contrasts the proud oppressor, whose desires are not upright, with the righteous person, who will live by their faithfulness: steady, loyal trust in God that holds on while the promised vision waits. The New Testament quotes it in Greek as “The one who is righteous will live by faith” (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11), to show that people are put right with God by trusting him, and Hebrews 10:38 uses it to urge believers not to draw back. Martin Luther’s reading of Romans 1:17 lay at the heart of the Reformation.

qa.question: Why does God use the Babylonians to judge Judah?
qa.answer: Habakkuk himself asks this (1:12–17). The book does not give a full explanation, but it makes three things plain: God is not approving Babylon’s cruelty, for chapter 2 pronounces five woes on it; Babylon’s power is temporary, for “the vision still waits for its appointed time”; and the LORD, not the empire, rules history, for “the LORD is in his holy temple; all the earth, be hushed before him” (2:20).

qa.question: What does “Though the fig tree does not flower” mean?
qa.answer: In Habakkuk 3:17–18 the prophet imagines every source of food in an ancient farming economy failing, the figs, grapes, olives, grain, sheep and cattle, as they would after an invasion, and declares that even then “yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will find joy in God, my Savior.” It is one of the Bible’s great statements of a faith that depends on God himself rather than on his gifts.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Look at the proud one: his desires are not upright within him; but the righteous will live by their faithfulness.

— Habakkuk 2:4

Most prophets speak to the people for God. Habakkuk spends most of his book speaking to God, and much of the time he is arguing. His three chapters are a conversation: two complaints, two answers, and a prayer. They begin with a cry that God is not listening and end with a song of joy in a ruined field. Between the two lies one of the most quoted sentences in the Old Testament.

The time

Habakkuk gives no king’s name and no date, but he tells us enough. God says, “For I am raising up the Chaldeans”, the people of southern Mesopotamia whose kings now ruled Babylon. Babylon threw off Assyrian rule in 626 BC, helped destroy Nineveh in 612, and defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605, becoming master of the region. Within twenty years its armies had destroyed Jerusalem. Habakkuk most likely prophesied in the last decades of Judah’s independence, perhaps in the reign of Jehoiakim (609–598 BC), when Babylon was rising and Judah’s own life was full of violence and injustice. Of the prophet himself we know nothing but his name, which has no certain meaning, and his calling: “Habakkuk the prophet”.

The shape of the book

  • 1:2–4: the first complaint. Why does God let violence and injustice go on in Judah?
  • 1:5–11: the first answer. He is raising up the Babylonians to judge it.
  • 1:12–17: the second complaint. How can a holy God use a nation more wicked than the one it punishes?
  • 2:1–20: the second answer. The vision will come in its time; the righteous will live by their faithfulness; and five woes fall on the proud.
  • Chapter 3: the prayer. A psalm of the God who comes to save, ending in trust.

“How long?”

The book opens with a question many people of faith have asked, and Habakkuk asks it without softening it:

How long, LORD, must I cry for help while you do not listen? I cry out to you, “Violence!” but you do not save.

— Habakkuk 1:2

He sees the instruction of God losing its force, the wicked hemming in the righteous, and “justice comes out twisted”. God’s answer is not what he expects. Something is coming that “you would not believe even if you were told”: the Chaldeans, swifter than leopards and fiercer than wolves at dusk, men “whose own strength is their god”. Centuries later Paul quoted this warning in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, so that his hearers would not be the scoffers it describes (Acts 13:41).

The answer only sharpens the problem. If Judah is bad, Babylon is worse. Habakkuk appeals to what he knows of God:

Your eyes are too pure to look on evil, and you cannot look on wrongdoing. Why then do you look on the treacherous, and keep silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than they?

— Habakkuk 1:13

He pictures the Babylonians as fishermen hauling nations up in nets and then burning incense to the net. Will it go on for ever? Then he does something worth noticing. He does not walk away. He says, “I will stand at my watchpost”, and waits for an answer.

The vision waits

God’s reply begins with an instruction to write:

Then the LORD answered me: Write down the vision; make it plain on tablets, so that whoever reads it can run. For the vision still waits for its appointed time; it hurries toward the end and will not prove false. Though it lingers, wait for it; it will certainly come and will not be late.

— Habakkuk 2:2–3

Then comes the heart of the book, the verse printed at the head of this introduction. The proud one, swollen with his own desires, stands on one side; on the other, “the righteous will live by their faithfulness”. The Hebrew word means firmness and steadiness, a loyal trust in God that holds on and shows itself in a faithful life. It is what Habakkuk himself is doing on the rampart.

The New Testament quotes the line three times, from its Greek form, as “The one who is righteous will live by faith” (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11; compare Hebrews 10:38). For Paul it shows that people are put right with God by trusting him, not by keeping the law. Reading Romans 1:17 in a monastery in Wittenberg, Martin Luther came to see the righteousness of God as a gift received by faith, a discovery that lay at the heart of the Reformation. The Hebrew and the Greek put the weight in slightly different places, one on faithfulness, one on faith, but they describe one life: the person who trusts God and keeps trusting him while the vision waits.

Five woes

The rest of chapter 2 is a taunt song that the nations will one day sing over Babylon. Five times it says “Woe”: to the one who piles up what is not his own, who builds his house high on wicked profit, who builds a city with bloodshed, who makes his neighbors drunk to shame them, and who prays to an idol of wood and stone. Even the building cries out against him: “The very stones will cry out from the wall”.

Twice the song lifts its eyes beyond Babylon. In the middle it promises:

For the earth will be as full of knowing the glory of the LORD as the sea is full of water.

— Habakkuk 2:14

And at the end, after the idol that has “no breath in it at all”, it turns to the living God: “But the LORD is in his holy temple; all the earth, be hushed before him.”

The prayer

Chapter 3 is a psalm, with the marks of one: a heading, the word Selah three times, and a note at the end for the music director. Habakkuk prays, “in wrath, remember mercy”, and then sees God coming from the south, from Teman and Mount Paran, as he came at Sinai, shaking the earth, splitting it with rivers, riding out “to save your people”. The vision leaves him trembling. But it also settles him: “Yet I will wait quietly for the day of trouble”. The prayer ends with the most famous lines in the book, a joy that does not depend on the harvest.

How to read Habakkuk

Read it as a conversation, and notice who is speaking in each part. It is short enough for one sitting. Mark the movement from “How long?” at the start to “yet I will rejoice” at the end, and ask what has changed. The Babylonians are still coming; the fields may still fail. What has changed is the prophet, who has brought his complaint to God, waited, and been given not an explanation but a vision of God himself.

Habakkuk gives every reader permission to ask hard questions, and shows where to take them: not away from God, but to him.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Habakkuk is poetry almost throughout, and it is printed here one line per line, as the poetry it is. A few of the translation’s choices are worth knowing.

“Faithfulness.” In 2:4 the translation says “by their faithfulness”, not “by faith”, because the Hebrew word means steady loyalty. Where the New Testament quotes the verse, it is translated from the Greek, whose word means faith or trust.

“The LORD.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, the four letters often written Yahweh, this translation writes “the LORD”; where the Hebrew joins it with the word for master, “the Lord GOD”, as in the last verse: “The Lord GOD is my strength”.

Words of worship. The musical terms of chapter 3, “shigionoth” and “Selah”, are left untranslated, as their exact meaning is no longer known.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Habakkuk 1
fields.body_html:
Habakkuk complains, and the LORD answers

1The oracle that Habakkuk the prophet saw.
2How long, LORD, must I cry for help while you do not listen?
I cry out to you, “Violence!” but you do not save.
3Why do you make me see wrongdoing? Why do you put up with trouble?
Ruin and violence are in front of me;
quarrels and conflict break out.
4So the instruction loses its force,
and justice never wins out.
The wicked hem in the righteous,
so justice comes out twisted.
5Look at the nations and watch,
and be utterly astonished!
For I am doing something in your days
that you would not believe even if you were told.
6For I am raising up the Chaldeans,
that fierce and reckless nation,
who sweep across the wide earth
to seize homes that are not their own.
7They are feared and dreaded;
they set their own law and claim their own honor.
8Their horses are swifter than leopards,
fiercer than wolves at dusk.
Their horsemen charge ahead;
their riders come from far away;
they swoop like an eagle rushing to devour.
9They all come intent on violence;
their faces are set straight ahead,
and they gather captives like sand.
10They scoff at kings
and make fun of rulers;
they laugh at every fortress,
for they pile up earth and take it.
11Then they sweep past like the wind and go on, guilty men
whose own strength is their god.
12Are you not from everlasting, LORD, my God, my Holy One? We will not die.
LORD, you have appointed them to execute judgment;
Rock, you have set them in place to bring correction.
13Your eyes are too pure to look on evil,
and you cannot look on wrongdoing.
Why then do you look on the treacherous,
and keep silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than they?
14You have made people like fish in the sea,
like creatures that crawl, with no ruler over them.
15The enemy pulls them all up with a hook;
he drags them away in his net
and gathers them in his fishing net;
so he rejoices and celebrates.
16So he offers sacrifices to his net
and burns incense to his fishing net,
for by them he lives in plenty
and eats the richest food.
17Will he keep on emptying his net,
killing nations without mercy, never stopping?
fields.summary: Habakkuk asks God how long violence and injustice will go on. God answers that the Babylonians are coming, and Habakkuk asks how God can use the wicked to punish those more righteous than they.

fields.title: Habakkuk 2
fields.body_html:
Write the vision

1I will stand at my watchpost
and take my place on the rampart.
I will look out to learn what he will say to me,
and how I should answer about my complaint.
2Then the LORD answered me:
Write down the vision; make it plain on tablets,
so that whoever reads it can run.
3For the vision still waits for its appointed time;
it hurries toward the end and will not prove false.
Though it lingers, wait for it;
it will certainly come and will not be late.
4Look at the proud one: his desires are not upright within him;
but the righteous will live by their faithfulness.
5Moreover, wine betrays the arrogant man;
he is never at rest.
He opens his throat as wide as Sheol; like death, he is never satisfied.
He gathers all the nations for himself
and collects all the peoples as his own.
6Will not all of them take up a mocking song against him,
with scorn and riddles about him, and say:
Woe to him who piles up what is not his own! How long will this go on?
He weighs himself down with goods taken in pledge!
7Will not your creditors rise up suddenly,
and those who make you tremble wake up?
Then you will become their plunder.
8Since you have looted many nations,
all the peoples who are left will loot you,
because of the human blood you shed and the violence against the land,
against the city and all who live in it.

Evil gain for his house

9Woe to him who gets wicked profit for his house,
to set his nest up high,
to be safe from the grasp of disaster!
10Your schemes have brought shame on your house;
by cutting off many peoples you have forfeited your own life.
11The very stones will cry out from the wall,
and a beam from the woodwork will answer them.

A city built with bloodshed

12Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed
and founds a town with wrongdoing!
13Has not the LORD of Armies decreed
that the peoples toil only for the fire
and the nations wear themselves out for nothing?
14For the earth will be as full of knowing the glory of the LORD
as the sea is full of water.

The cup of shame

15Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink,
pouring out his fury until they are drunk,
so that he can gaze at their nakedness!
16You will be filled with shame instead of glory.
Drink, you too, and be exposed as uncircumcised!
The cup in the right hand of the LORD will come around to you,
and disgrace will cover your glory.
17The violence you did to Lebanon will overwhelm you,
and so will the slaughter that terrified its animals,
because of the human blood you shed and the violence against the land,
against the city and all who live in it.

Idols that cannot speak

18What use is an idol once its maker has carved it,
or a metal image, a teacher of lies?
Its maker trusts in what he himself has shaped
when he fashions idols that cannot speak.

19Woe to him who says to a piece of wood, “Wake up!”
or to a lifeless stone, “Get up!”
Can it teach?
It is covered with gold and silver,
but there is no breath in it at all.
20But the LORD is in his holy temple;
all the earth, be hushed before him.
fields.summary: God tells Habakkuk to write the vision plainly, for it will surely come; the righteous will live by their faithfulness. Five woes are pronounced on the proud oppressor.

fields.title: Habakkuk 3
fields.body_html:
Habakkuk’s prayer

1A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, on shigionoth.
2LORD, I have heard of your fame, and I stand in awe.
LORD, renew your work in our own time;
in our own time make it known;
in wrath, remember mercy.
3God came from Teman,
the Holy One from Mount Paran.
His splendor covered the heavens,
and the earth was filled with his praise. Selah
4His brightness was like the sunlight;
rays flashed from his hand,
and there his power lay hidden.
5Disease went ahead of him,
and plague followed at his heels.
6He stood, and the earth shook; he looked, and the nations trembled.
The ancient mountains broke apart;
the age-old hills sank down.
His ways are eternal.
7I saw the tents of Cushan in distress;
the tent curtains of Midian shook.

God rides out to save

8Was your anger burning against the rivers, LORD?
Was your wrath against the streams,
or your fury against the sea,
as you rode your horses,
your chariots of salvation?
9Your bow was drawn from its case;
the arrows were charged by your word.
You split the earth with rivers. Selah
10The mountains saw you and writhed;
a torrent of water swept past;
the deep roared aloud
and lifted its hands high.
11Sun and moon stood still in the heavens
at the light of your flying arrows,
at the flash of your gleaming spear.
12In fury you strode across the earth;
in anger you trampled the nations.
13You went out to save your people,
to save your anointed one.
You crushed the head of the house of the wicked,
stripping it bare from the foundation up to the neck. Selah

Waiting quietly and rejoicing

14With his own arrows you pierced the head of his warriors
when they stormed out to scatter me,
gloating as if about to devour
the helpless in their hiding place.
15You trampled the sea with your horses,
churning the mighty waters.
16I heard, and my body trembled; my lips quivered at the sound.
Decay entered my bones, and my legs shook beneath me.
Yet I will wait quietly for the day of trouble
to come on the people who invade us.
17Though the fig tree does not flower and the vines bear no grapes,
though the olive harvest fails
and the fields yield nothing to eat,
though the sheep vanish from the pen
and the stalls hold no cattle,
18yet I will rejoice in the LORD;
I will find joy in God, my Savior.
19The Lord GOD is my strength;
he makes my feet as sure as a deer’s
and lets me walk on the heights.
For the music director. With stringed instruments.
fields.summary: Habakkuk prays for God to remember mercy in wrath and describes God’s coming in power. Though the fig tree does not flower, he will rejoice in God his savior.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Though the fig tree does not flower and the vines bear no grapes, though the olive harvest fails and the fields yield nothing to eat, though the sheep vanish from the pen and the stalls hold no cattle, yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will find joy in God, my Savior. The Lord GOD is my strength; he makes my feet as sure as a deer’s and lets me walk on the heights. For the music director. With stringed instruments.

— Habakkuk 3:17–19

Habakkuk ends where farmers in Judah feared most to be: a fig tree with no blossom, empty vines, failed olives, bare fields, an empty sheep pen. It is a picture of what the Babylonian invasion would leave behind. And in the middle of it the prophet sings.

The question the book leaves with you

Habakkuk never gets the explanation he asked for. He is not told why the wicked prosper for a time, or why God chose such a crooked instrument to judge his people. He is given a promise that the vision will come at its appointed time, a sentence about how the righteous live while they wait, and a sight of God himself. That turns out to be enough.

So the question the book leaves is not whether we can understand what God is doing, but whether we will trust him when we cannot. “Though it lingers, wait for it”. The book’s answer is the word “yet”: though everything fails, “yet I will rejoice in the LORD”. That is not a mood. It is a decision, made on the rampart, by a man whose legs were still shaking.

Where it points

The New Testament takes Habakkuk’s central line and builds on it. Paul writes that in the gospel the righteousness of God is revealed, “As it is written, ‘The one who is righteous will live by faith.’” (Romans 1:17), and Hebrews urges believers who are tempted to give up not to draw back, because “the one who is coming will arrive and will not be slow in coming” (Hebrews 10:37). The vision Habakkuk waited for has a face. And the hope of 2:14, an earth full of the knowledge of the LORD’s glory, is the hope of the whole Bible.

Where to go from here

A few places in this library to take Habakkuk further:

  • On joy when the fields fail (3:17–19). The Prayers Jesus Learned, an Ochorus Original, whose chapter “Though the Fig Tree Does Not Flower” walks through the whole book; and Hannah Whitall Smith’s The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life, whose chapter “A Lesson in the Interior Life” is built around Habakkuk’s song (3:17–19).
  • On asking God why (1:2–4, 1:12–17). The Key Teachings of Elisabeth Elliot, an Ochorus Original, and its chapter “On Asking God Why”.
  • On “in wrath, remember mercy” (3:2). Charles G. Finney’s sermon What a Revival of Religion Is, on Habakkuk 3:2, and Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s The Cry for Revival (Psalm 85:6).
  • On living by faith (2:4). The Key Teachings of Martin Luther, an Ochorus Original, whose chapter “The Righteousness of God” tells how Romans 1:17 changed Luther’s life; John Calvin’s Commentary on Romans, on Romans 1:17; and John Wesley’s sermon Salvation by Faith (Ephesians 2:8).
  • Two evening and morning readings. Charles H. Spurgeon’s Evening by Evening, September 10, on “Evening wolves” (Habakkuk 1:8), and his Morning by Morning, December 12, on “His ways are everlasting” (Habakkuk 3:6).
  • On Habakkuk and Christ. Augustine’s The City of God, Book XVIII, chapters 31 and 32, on Habakkuk’s vision and on his prayer and song.

And read Romans and Galatians in this same edition, where Habakkuk’s sentence becomes the hinge of Paul’s gospel.

Every reference to Habakkuk in this library can be tapped to read the verse. But the best next step may be to return to the watchpost with your own questions, and to remember where the prophet’s second chapter ends:

But the LORD is in his holy temple; all the earth, be hushed before him.

— Habakkuk 2:20
